content.text: I'll expand all three elided regions, since editing `planStructural` means touching the seams (options/types), the grammar-loading helpers it calls, and the helper functions the planner is built out of.

I've expanded all three regions. Here's the orientation on `planStructural`, then the parts that will bite you when editing.

## The call chain

```
StructuralPlanner.plan
  └─ planStructural(input, options)          ← seam checks + parser lifecycle
       ├─ assertStructuralLanguage(input.language)   → GrammarUnavailableError
       ├─ MissingMarkerPricingError if input.pricing is undefined (JS-caller backstop)
       ├─ loadGrammar(language)  →  new Parser() / parser.parse()
       └─ planFromTree(tree, input, options, language)   ← all the actual planning
            ├─ profileFor(language).structure!          (non-null is proven by the assert)
            ├─ unitsOf(root, text, structure)           → readonly Unit[]
            ├─ matchUnits(units, input, options)        → readonly boolean[]
            ├─ utf8OffsetIndex(text, unit starts+ends)  → UTF-16 → UTF-8 map
            ├─ pass 1: maximalRuns(units, matched) → collapse(run) | refused.push(run)
            └─ pass 2 (budget rung): bestSubRun(refusedRun, collapse, pricing, spanBytes, enough)
```

`planStructural` itself is thin: it is the refusal seam (unsupported language, missing pricing, null tree) plus `try/finally` tree and parser disposal. All policy lives in `planFromTree`.

## The load-bearing ideas

**The `Unit` is the atom.** `unitsOf` groups each top-level declaration with its attached doc comment (and, in Rust, its outer attributes) into a single kept-or-collapsed-whole record. That's why "a kept declaration keeps its doc comment" is structural rather than a post-hoc range patch. `Unit` holds only numbers and strings — no `Node` references — which is what makes the `finally { tree?.delete() }` safe.

**`collapse` is the single minting point.** Every elision in both passes goes through the closure in `planFromTree`: one legality rule (`minSiblings`, the line-comment/`restOfLineIsBlank` check), one price (`savingBytes(candidate, pricing) > 0`), one explanation (`explain`). The budget rung physically cannot cut something pass 1 would have refused, because it calls the same closure.

**Safety is a property of shape, not of checks.** `maximalRuns` never emits a run containing a matched or pinned unit, so no sub-run of any refused run can contain one either. There is no "don't cut the focus match" guard anywhere downstream — don't add one, and don't add a code path that builds candidate groups outside `maximalRuns`/`bestSubRun`.

**Two passes, budget-triggered.** Pass 1 takes every profitable maximal run. Only if `predictOutputBytes(...) > input.budgetBytes` does the rung re-ask each *refused* run for its best profitable sub-run, earliest-first, stopping as soon as the plan fits. Maximal runs are preferred because one marker naming everything it hid is a better explanation than two naming halves.

## Editing hazards

1. **`bestSubRun`'s two bounds are exact only under current assumptions.** The span bound (`spanBytes(...) <= bestSaving → break`) is sound solely because a cut can never save more than the bytes it spans, and because both loops walk spans monotonically (start-ascending, length-descending). If you make `collapse` produce a range wider than the group's span, or change the enumeration order, both breaks become heuristic and can skip a winner. The `enough` early-return likewise depends on that order defining "earliest, longest". This bound is not cosmetic — the comment records 159 KB / 131 s before it existed, on tool-controlled input, on the over-budget path that is the normal case.

2. **`toByte` only contains unit boundaries.** It's seeded from `units.flatMap(u => [u.start, u.end])`, and every lookup uses `.get(x)!`. Any new range boundary you introduce must be added to that seed or you get a silent `undefined`.

3. **UTF-16 in, UTF-8 out.** All internal positions are JS code-unit indices; conversion happens once, at the end. Safe only because every converted index is a parse-node boundary (hence a character boundary).

4. **Never add a lexical fallback.** Three sites say so (class doc, `planStructural` doc, `assertStructuralLanguage`'s message). Output labelled `structural/v1` that is really line windows is undetectable from outside.

5. **`isStructuralLanguage` is shared with the `auto` strategy** (`plan/auto.ts`). One membership test, deliberately — a second spelling lets `auto` route a language that `assertStructuralLanguage` then refuses.

6. **`STRUCTURAL_LANGUAGES` is guarded.** `test/guards/structural-totality.test.ts` requires a fixture, snapshot and doc-comment case per language listed.

7. **Coupled pairs that drift silently:** `SIBLING_COLLAPSE_RULE` ↔ whatever `pricing` prices; `explain`'s kind labels ↔ `NON_DECLARATION_KINDS` (an unlisted non-declaration kind makes a mixed marker claim "declarations" and overclaim about the tree).

8. **Determinism is a contract:** same text/language/focus/options ⇒ byte-identical plan. Note `saving > bestSaving` (strict) is the tie-break that keeps the earliest, longest candidate — flipping it to `>=` changes output.

9. **`budgetBytes` is a target, not a guarantee.** Under the last profitable cut, the only remaining bytes are the declarations the caller asked to keep. Don't "fix" this by dropping focus matches; callers check `outputBytes`.

One small thing worth confirming before you edit: `planFromTree` reads `const pricing = input.pricing` and passes it to `bestSubRun` as `MarkerPricing`, relying on `planStructural` having already thrown `MissingMarkerPricingError`. If you ever call `planFromTree` from a new entry point, that check must come with it.
